syntax.syntax_item: [L, U, P, Q] = lu(S, thresh, outputForm)

param_input_item.param_description: a matrix (square or rectangular): single or double, real or complex, dense or sparse.
a character vector or string: 'matrix' (default) or 'vector'. Any leading part of either word is accepted, in any case.
a sparse matrix: single or double, real or complex.
pivot threshold between 0 and 1: a scalar with three outputs or fewer (default 1), a scalar or a vector of two elements with four or five outputs (default [0.1, 0.001]).

param_output_item.param_description: Lower triangular factor: matrix (same type A)
Upper triangular factor: matrix (same type A).
Row permutation: real matrix (same precision as A), or row vector of double when outputForm is 'vector'.
Column permutation: real sparse matrix (same precision as S), or row vector of double when outputForm is 'vector'.
Row scaling: real sparse diagonal matrix (same precision as S).

description.p: [L, U] = lu(A) function decomposes a full matrixA into two matrices: an upper triangular matrixU and a permuted lower triangular matrix L.
This factorization satisfies the equation A = L * U.
[L, U, P] = lu(A) function, when used with three output arguments, provides a permutation matrixP in addition to the unit lower triangular matrixL and the upper triangular matrix U.
This factorization is expressed as A = P'LU, where L is unit lower triangular, and U is upper triangular.
Sparse double, single, complex double, and complex single matrices are supported. Sparse factors keep sparse storage and keep the input numeric class where applicable.
With outputForm set to 'vector', P is returned as a row vector p of row indices such that A(p, :) = L * U.
[L, U, P, Q] = lu(S) for a sparse matrix S also returns a column permutation Q chosen to keep L and U sparse, with P * S * Q = L * U.

[L, U, P, Q, D] = lu(S) also returns a diagonal scaling matrix D with P * (D \ S) * Q = L * U. Each diagonal entry of D is the sum of the absolute values (|real part| + |imaginary part|) of a row of S, or 1 for an empty row.

thresh controls pivoting for sparse matrices. With three outputs or fewer, the current row stays as pivot when its magnitude is at least thresh times the largest candidate; 1 gives partial pivoting. With four or five outputs, thresh(1) is the pivot tolerance among rows and thresh(2) the tolerance used to keep a diagonal pivot. Lower values favour sparsity over numerical stability.
With outputForm set to 'vector', Q is also returned as a row vector q such that S(p, q) = L * U.
For a sparse matrix, a column without a usable pivot gives a zero on the diagonal of U; no error is raised.
NaN and Inf values are accepted and spread through the factors. The pivot is the first entry of largest magnitude in its column, so a NaN becomes a pivot only when it is the first candidate.

For a sparse A with three outputs or fewer, a NaN candidate is always the pivot, the one with the lowest row index first. With four or five outputs, a NaN in the column makes the pivot threshold test fail for every row, and the pivot is the diagonal entry or the row with the fewest entries.

Dense matrices with at most 16 rows and columns (8 for complex data) are factored by an unblocked algorithm that rounds every operation in a fixed order, without fused multiply-add, so the factors are the same on every platform. Larger matrices use LAPACK.

xmldoc.used_function: LAPACK dgetrf, LAPACK sgetrf, LAPACK zgetrf, LAPACK cgetrf

example_item.example_item_data: A = magic(5) [L, U] = lu(A) L * U
A = magic(5) [L, U, P] = lu(A); subplot(1, 2, 1) spy(L) title('L factor') subplot(1, 2, 2) spy(U) title('U factor')
